utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to call its next expert witness. That would be Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I just want to say that I don't have any translation on the channel. I know that B/C/S is usually on channel number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Still no translation, Ms. Pilipovic? You receive translation, General Galic? You can now hear me in a language you understand, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mundis, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, perhaps while the witness is being brought into the courtroom I can briefly address the issue of a motion which the Prosecution filed on the 6th of February concerning the request for reconsideration of the admission of the expert report of Dr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the -- there is a draft being prepared at this very moment so it has our full attention. I couldn't tell you but it's, I would say, a matter of days that you will receive the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you are Professor Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. I see that you have the text already in your hands may I advise you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Professor Dunjic. You will first be examined by the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I start asking you questions, could you introduce yourself and give us why you are full name, could you tell us when you were born and what your area of interest is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Dunjic, I was born in 1950 in Belgrade. That's where I graduated from the faculty of medicine. I am a doctor of medicine. I received a Ph.D and masters and I am a specialist in forensic medicine. At the moment I am the director of the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Belgrade. To date I have published over 160 professional articles which concern all areas of forensic medicine. I have written -- I have published several books that have to do with forensic pathology, I have written a text book which I published on an independent basis for medical students and I have also written a book which has to do with forensic pathology and with issues with forensic medicine that relate to school, the school in the European Centre for Peace and Development. It relates to certain problems that arise when applying traditional medicine. I am also the coauthor of a book that deals with the theme of subject -- the theme of suicide. This book has been printed and reprinted as a whole by the Russian academy of science. I have a special chapter that deals with forensic matters in surgery with emergency medicine with -- I am the coauthor of these books. I am also the coauthor of an interesting book that was published and which resulted from one of the projects that I've been involved in up to now and it deals with the victims of torture, with people who were in camps in Croatia and Bosnia, this book was published in English and I have brought it with me. So I have been exclusively involved in the field of forensic pathology and in the field of everything that has to do with forensic medicine. In addition, as an expert, I've worked on several occasions in Kosovo in 1998. I studied cases that concerned people who were killed in the village of Glodjane and in 1999 in the village of Racak and in 2001 and 2002 as the chief of an expert team I was present at all exhumations that were carried out in Batajnica. As far as my social activities are concerned, I am a member of the Association for Forensic Medicine in Yugoslavia and also in the former Yugoslavia I've organised several congresses. I participated and directed several projects that have to do with forensic pathology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Regardless of the fact that in addition to your report which we have provided to the Trial Chamber, we also provided your curriculum vitae but thank you for mentioning all these details.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise but I forgot to say - just a minute, it's among my papers - I've been engaged here for the needs of the Tribunal on several occasions, so I had to remind myself of this. In the case of Dusko Tadic, IT-91-1 [sic], I provided an expert report for the Defence. I also worked in the Foca group, IT-96-23, I made an expert at the request of the Tribunal, it had to do with Zoran Vukovic who was in the Foca group. On two occasions I examined the cases of Zoran Simic in the case IT-95-9-PT. I've been engaged in this case by you and I was also engaged by the Defence in the Plavsic/Krajisnik case, IT-00-39-I-40. I also worked with the Prosecution and this had to do with all the cases that I already mentioned and which relate to body parts that were found in the village of Glodjane and in the village of Radjak in 1998 and in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, at the request of Defence counsel, you compiled a report which you completed in October 2002. My question is as follows, is there anything that you would like to modify or anything that you would like to add to the report that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, there is nothing that I would like to add. I've examined all the material so it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of material you used when compiling your report what material is your report based on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I made a list with the case manager and it has been provided to the Trial Chamber, a list for each incident that has been listed here. I have to say that Defence counsel provided me with medical documentation, primarily with medical documentation and statements of witnesses who have been heard here. I was also provided with certain police reports which were among these documents slight -- at a little -- a little later I was provided with photographs, video recordings and I have to say that I didn't receive all this material at the same time. But I was provided with this material at intervals and I had to examine it in this way. I'd also like to mention that I forgot to do so when I was introducing myself. For this case, I also went to Sarajevo on two occasions and I visited certain locations there which have been mentioned in these cases here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us about the material that Defence counsel provided you with, you mentioned medical documentation, you mentioned witness statements, police report, photographs, video recordings, was there anything else that you used? If we're talking about witness statements, which statements did you take into consideration in particular?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, above all the statements that were in the transcript, but I have to say that I also used statements that were provided at the beginning of this case so that in cases where I had to compare findings, medical findings and these witness statements, that's what I used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you went to Sarajevo on two occasions, can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I went there together with certain ballistics experts, people who represent the Defence in this case in order to have a look at these sites where these incidents took place and have a direct knowledge to gain information about the possibility of projectiles falling there, hitting these places which wounded the victims that have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us what kind of material you used in order to compile your report, can you now tell us what the basis of your report is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, the basis of any forensic medical report is the medical documentation, if such documentation exists, so this is the basis one uses in order to assess wounds, in order to assess the number of wounds, the nature of the wounds, these are the things that will be used in a subsequent analysis or when compiling a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you've told us, and that the medical documentation is the basis upon which you compiled your report. Can you tell us, when compiling your report, you examined all the cases which are mentioned in the indictment, you only said that you didn't mention incident number 1. Can you tell us whether with regard to all the cases whether you had medical documentation for all of the cases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to point out to the Trial Chamber that I carefully analysed the medical documentation that related to all these incidents that was mentioned in connection with all these incidents and I arrived at the conclusion that in certain cases, there was no medical documentation whatsoever. I was only able to analyse the witness statements, either the statements of witness who had been heard or the statements of victims so if we are talking about medical documentation, I could mention three categories. We have a group of medical documents which either concerns a letter which releases someone from hospital or a short case history, a photocopy of a case history, another group of documents would be death certificates and the third group of documents, the third category would include statements after post mortem had been performed. In fact there was not a record of the post mortem, the autopsy report, there would just be a diagnosis relating to the wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, bearing in mind you said there was three categories of documents, can you tell us whether the medical documents that you used were sufficient for your purpose? Were you able to compile your report on the basis of these documents? Did these documents contain sufficient information for you to compile your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to point out in the medical documentation that relates to all the cases mentioned here, not a single medical document is not sufficient and can't be used for forensic purposes and I'm also referring to the first group of medical documents when I express such a position.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, tell us -- we're talking about the quality of the medical documents. That's a document which was part of the first group, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document belongs to the first group, so there are two shortcomings here. The first one is a purely technical nature it's not a very good copy, it's not very legible. The second shortcoming concerns its contents and the extent to which it is valid for the Trial Chamber. A diagnosis has been clearly mentioned here, it says "vulnus transsclopetarium" and then it mentions the part of the body, "regium frontalis femuris", et cetera. On the basis of that it is a medical diagnosis of the wound to a certain part of the body, but that part can't be used for forensic purposes, that means that on the basis of such a medical document, I can't provide a valid piece of evidence with regard to the question as to where the projectile actually came from. I can't say whether there's one or several wounds, I can't say where the entry wound is located or where the exit wound is located. So there is nothing that I can say that would be valid or useful for the Trial Chamber or for my report. Nothing I could say on the basis of this diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, bearing in mind that this medical document was made during a period, it was a wartime period in that area, can you tell us, given that you have told us how valuable such a document might be, did you personally have the opportunity of seeing documents, other documents that had to do with that area or present in that area in the relevant time period and can you tell us what your conclusion is? We know what your conclusions are on the basis of your report, but can you tell us about the documents that you were able to analyse?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to say that because I'm dealing with these problems which is the injury by firearms, for us, forensic specialists, what's very important is that all relevant data about an injury have to be entered and be part of the medical documentation. On this occasion, I do not wish to attack my colleagues, doctors, that they are not writing the medical documentation as they should because their primary purpose is to treat the wounded which is perfectly normal but in this context, in this medical documentation, I've had the opportunity to look and peruse a great deal of medical documentation of those wounded who were brought to the Kasindol hospital which is from the period of 1991-1992 that is from 1992 to 1995 where they were treated at the surgical department, the injured were treated there. The medical documentation that you have mentioned we have done an expert report a month ago, this medical documentation can be categorised in the same way as the first group of this medical documentation that we were just talking about. So these injuries are listed and the treatment, the intervention of the doctor was also mentioned but the actual description of the injury, and the -- how the wound was treated does not give us, the forensic specialists, to give answers that the Trial Chamber needs, that is, when an expert report is required. So this medical document is important, it does talk about the wound, the wound is there, but there is nothing else apart from that. So for a medical document, to have a legal standing, to have legal value for a Trial Chamber, it has to have certain -- it has to be made compiled according to certain criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the answer of Professor Dunjic, when he -- the way he has qualified the medical documentation and bearing in mind that the Professor just told us that he had the opportunity to peruse the documentation, Kasindol hospital and he has carried out the examination of those documents, the Defence would like to just show, without tendering these documents, we'd like to just show some documents for which we would like to have the Professor's opinion. The Defence has --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would object on the grounds of relevance to this entire exercise and if you'd like me to explain the reasons why I would request to do so in the absence of the witness assuming he speaks or understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you would like to explain that, I will have to ask you, Professor Dunjic, to leave the courtroom for a while. I take it that you read or understand some English. Yes, which is -- since the Prosecution would like to explain something in your absence, I invite you to leave the courtroom together with the usher for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has told us this afternoon that the documents that he did rely upon were insufficient for forensic purposes. The Prosecution would assert that the procedure which the Defence is wishing to undertake would involve showing this witness medical documents from another hospital or from a clinic to which none of the victims in this case were sent for treatment and ask him to undertake a comparative analysis of the quality of those documents, vis-a-vis the documents, the medical documentation that is in evidence before this Trial Chamber. The Prosecution would assert that there is little or no value in him doing so in light of his previous testimony that the documents that he did review were not sufficient for forensic purposes. To have him then review documents from clinic which did meet his criteria, the Prosecution asserts, would serve little or no value whatsoever to the issues before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence wished to show Professor Dunjic the documents, a couple of documents, that the professor had the opportunity of seeing and giving his opinion on and by showing these documents, we would like to demonstrate that Professor Dunjic gave his analysis in an objective way because his opinion, when we're talking about documentation, the medical documentation, it can also -- is also valid for the hospital that was under the control of the Muslims as well as the hospital that was under the control of the Serbs. So that's why we believe that the credibility of Professor Dunjic can be checked in this way and bearing in mind the testimony of Defence witnesses who have testified so far, and who have testified about the medical documentation that exists, in the sense of injuries caused by firearms, also on this side under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, we wish to support the thesis of the Defence that in that area, there was fighting, combat on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. A couple of quick observations. In the first instance, the Prosecution is not objecting to this procedure on the grounds that Professor Dunjic is anything other than objective. Again, the basis was that he has testified that the documents that he did review were not of sufficient quality to allow him to undertake a forensic analysis. Second of all, as my learned colleague has just raised the issue of injuries on the side under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska and in fact the documents which she is proposing to show to this witness relate to injuries of Bosnian Serbs on the Serb-controlled side of the confrontation line, and the Prosecution, again, Mr. President, would contend that this entire exercise is of little or no relevance whatsoever to the issues before this Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber allows you to ask questions about one example of the other side, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Defence will present one medical document and I had it translated and the booths have it as well. This is document number two, just to help my colleague because I just handed the document to him just before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and may I ask you to very much restrict yourself to the field of expertise of Professor Dunjic which is not how much fighting was going on where, although I do understand that if you have patients at one side of the confrontation line that it might be considered to be likely that they came from that part of the confrontation line but let's take advantage of the specific expertise of Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Here, I have six copies of document number one so I think that will be sufficient so it's document number one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, before this short break, you talked to us about the value of medical documentation and you told us that you had the opportunity of perusing the medical documentation from the Kasindol hospital. The Defence will show you one document and, bearing in mind your experience, could you please tell us if you had the opportunity of analysing, examining such a document, would you be able to tell us about its value, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I had to read it first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: These are two documents that you have before you, this documents is a letter of discharge which was compiled for a patient that was treated in hospital, his initials, dates, location and so on. At the end there is a diagnosis and the diagnosis is in Latin. I am going to read it very quickly and translate it. So, this is a firearm wound in the area of the left ear and the lower jaw area on the left-hand side and there were parts of fractured bones, that's what it says in Latin. On the second page is an excerpt about how the injury occurred and everything that was done. From this document, as I have already explained, belongs to this first group of medical documents where I can only find out that the certain person, name and surname, in this period that is given, was treated and that person had suffered a firearm injury somewhere on the left half of their face. Now, if you ask me to explain whether this is an injury with one projectile and what type of the projectile this injury was caused, what was the position of the person that was injured at the moment when that person was injured, I cannot answer that question. If you ask me how far or, that is, the distance between the firing position and the body, saying that this injury was caused by a firearm, whether it was with a shorter barrel or a long barrel, again, I couldn't answer that question. And this is, conditionally speaking, medical documentation which can be used during an expert report, expert examination but from which we cannot use it so that it can have an evidentiary value for the Trial Chamber. And in this case, I would do exactly the same which is exactly what I did when I was analysing in these other cases, as in these cases. So what I would have to do or whoever does these things in terms of forensic experts there would have to be an additional x-ray, an additional examination and a detailed description of the wound from which I could then draw what I can talk about in relation to the injuries where you can ask me questions and I can give you the relevant answer. So this is the identical type of examination which cannot be very useful for an expert report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. So, so far, you first spoken to us about what you call the first group of documents. You've told us that the medical documentation in your opinion, the one that you've used that you have categorised it, I think what you called the death certificate group, and you also gave a third group of documents. Can you tell us, this second group of medical documents that you tell us these are death certificates, what is the value of such documents? And did you have the opportunity that while you were doing your expert report, did you also have such documents at your disposal when we were speaking about the incidents that you examined for the expert report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In these cases that I analysed individually, I did come across, conditionally speaking, medical documents about -- which were death certificates. These are kind of forms that are filled in by the doctor but most of the time it's filled in by some other person, a layperson, a non-medical person filling in certain data about the person who died and the one -- in one box, that person says what is the cause of death, it's a kind of layman's opinion without an autopsy, without an examination diagnosis is written, that is, either vulnus sclopetarium, that is, the firearm wound so on and the region. So on the basis of this diagnosis this is the same diagnosis as it is in the other group of documents. So it's a diagnosis from which I cannot give you any answers if you ask me some questions. I can only say that this is such and such a person who died and possibly I can see that if there is a cause of death which has not been established in a proper way. So in this document, I can't possibly use now in order to explain to you how that person came to be injured, with which weapon, how many wounds this person had, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. So my following question would be the third group of documents that you had the opportunity to use during the compiling of your expert report and can you tell us something about the value of these documents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In the third group of documents, there were reports, there were also official medical documents that were issued by the administration of the forensics institute in Sarajevo. Because I am a director of the forensics institute in Belgrade, I know that we do not issue such certificates as a rule to the court. In this certificate which I looked at it just gives the diagnosis of the cause of death and one injury is listed as proof that this person had been autopsied and that this was the cause of death but now I don't have a document. I don't have the autopsy report, a record of the autopsy from which I could assess how this injury occurred, whether there was just one injury because plural was often used so it could mean there were several projectiles or was it a projectile from a firearm or was it shrapnel and so on. So this document is only valid in the sense that it confirms one medical procedure was carried out, like autopsy and that death was certified in relation to an injury but there is nothing else that could be valid for an expert report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When you gave us your position about the value of the medical documentation that you used, can you tell us in compiling your expert report and you told us you also had the opportunity to read the statements of witnesses that were given to the investigators, and also the testimonies of witnesses that you were also able to look at the video material and that you were able to look at the photographs. Can you tell us, looking at those sources that you used, how much were you able to get from such documents? How valuable were the facts that you got from those sources for your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The testimony of a witness that is -- that testifies either it's a witness or it's the injured person, these testimonies are taken by an expert as a kind of reference. In a sense that the testimony would help me to establish the position of the body as defined by the person who was injured in relation to a -- some relevant medical documentation and that is why I looked over the video material, the photographs, and I have also read the statements, the testimonies. And what is interesting here is that as far as the medical documentation is concerned, it doesn't correspond to, for instance, the statement, the testimony of a given witness and I have -- would like to show what I am talking about. This is about incident number 4, this is a Witness G, this is a protected witness but I would like to show you what I mean. I can do you a sketch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, bearing in mind the answer of the professor, and his position in relation to such a situation, the Defence would like to first, of course, with your leave, show the video materials so that we can all be reminded of incident number 4. And also, bearing in mind that this was a protected witness, this is Witness G, so this is incident number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may play the video. We'll do that and then -- closed session or ... We are in closed session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, we are not yet. Ms. Pilipovic, do you have the P number for that video, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I think that's P3280AA -- A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you use the English version of the report because we don't know which version you'll use, Professor Dunjic. Are you going to use the original version or are you going to use the English version of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. It's all the same to me. We can also use the English version of the medical document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it's very difficult to cover wherever the name appears.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary, Your Honour. I won't show it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and could you please read those parts of the statement that is relevant because I do understand that you want to draw our attention to contradictions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may the document please be returned to -- it will not be put on the ELMO and you are not going to read the name of the person wherever it appears, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Just a minute. No, the drawing. I'll show it here. We can see the position of the body, at the important point in time. This arrow indicates the direction the projectile came from according to the witness. That's something that we just saw in the video. In the medical documentation -- that's the witness' statement that -- but in the medical documentation, it says that the person in question was wounded through the right hemithorax, the 5th thoracic or rather cervical point and that that projectile passed through a part of the left thorax, that is what it says. What I've read out from the medical document can be presented in the following way, Your Honour, the right hemithorax, the spine and the left part of the left thorax that would mean the projectile entered the body in this manner. So we have the medical facts and we have the witness' statement which don't agree, these two elements don't agree. Either he wasn't facing this way when he was wounded when the witness was wounded or the projectile came from the other side, not the side that he indicated. This medical documentation is not sufficient. The medical documentation doesn't say what the passage of the projectile was when passing through the body and it doesn't say whether it passed through the body, doesn't say whether there was an exit wound. The point between the entry, the place where there was contact with the bone and the exit wound on the basis of these three points we can establish the channel and establish what the direction of the projectile was when passing through the body and on the basis of the video that we have seen, and given what the witness said with regard to the direction of the projectile, well obviously there is a difference and as a forensics expert, I've pointed out what should be done in order to clarify this matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, your conclusion with regard to this incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would very much appreciate if it could see the video once more, even if it would be without sound which distracts our attention from -- oh, yes, we have to turn it to closed session again. Perhaps we could look at the video just before the break so that we lose only half so we'll now continue and then just before we have the break, we'll have the curtains down, look at the video again and then they can be open again during the break. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, with regard to this incident and your conclusion, on the basis of the witness' statement and on the basis of the medical documents related to this incident, you have told us that it is essential to examine the victim in order to determine the point of the entry wound and the exit wound with precision and everything else that has to be determined, for example, whether it was -- whether the projectile was fired in a direct manner and to determine what kind of projectile was concerned; have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you have just told us that it's not possible to rely on the witness statements or you've told us about the extent to which it's possible to rely on it and on the extent on which it's possible to rely on the medical documentation. I would like to focus on what ballistics experts could say about the wounds, the direction of the projectile and about determining the location from which the projectile was fired on. These are the issues I would like to concentrate on. My question is as follows: What does an expert report on the projectile include in your opinion, if one wants to obtain a precise answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The question included a statement focussing on ballistics expertise and I'm not of the view that this witness is qualified as a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, given that we have heard a ballistics expert, and in response to our questions, he said how it was essential for there to be cooperation between ballistics experts and forensic medicine experts, perhaps I should have asked the professor what has to be done if an expert report has to be compiled about wounds inflicted from firearms and in order for this report to be acceptable. I was thinking about the testimony of our ballistics expert and it's in that sense that I put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Ms. Pilipovic, if you are talking about what would be needed in order to make an expert report, I think it would be of some importance to know what expert report you had in mind. Are you asking this witness what would be needed for a ballistic expert report or are you asking this witness about what would be needed for a medical expert report, forensic medicine? I think you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. To provide a report in cases of wounds inflicted by firearms, reports compiled by experts in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I am an expert in forensic medicine and I also deal with ballistics that have to do with wounds so in a certain sense I am a ballistics expert but only within the field that concerns and relates to wounds inflicted on the human body. So when we are provided with a case as forensic experts and when we have to analyse the documents, this includes cooperation with ballistics experts and other technical experts who have to be involved in examining the case. I do my bit, but the bit that I have to do as a forensics expert relates to examining the body and determining, with precision, the wound, the location of the wound. It's necessary to locate the point of the entry wound, the existence of the channel, the wound channel, but before I start my work, it's necessary to establish certain traces which can be found around the entry wound. I have to control this in order to be able to use the results when compiling an expert report. So analysing the distance from which fire was opened and all the traces that can be found on the body and on the clothes of the victim. After that has done it's necessary to perform an autopsy in order examine the wounded person and this has to include all the relevant facts and this should include photographs, certain other methods, et cetera, et cetera, and after this has been done, you have to analyse the records, you have to analyse the witness statements which are relevant as far as the way in which the wound was inflicted and then as ballistics experts and forensic experts, once all of these elements have been gathered and analyzed, together with the judge, the Defence, the Prosecution, we then go to the site and we reconstruct the event at the site and it's only after we have carried out all this work, after the ballistics work has been done, the forensic work has been done, only after this has been done you can proceed to reconstruct the event and you try to ensure that all the elements agree with each other. I say that the traces on the sites, we have reports on the traces found at the sites, traces of blood, cartridges, gun powder, et cetera, I do everything, I do the work that concerns biological traces as a forensic expert and the ballistics expert has to do with analyzing the ammunition, the rifle, et cetera, this is what he has to do and then we analyze the records together and if necessary, we reconstruct the event with the Court. This is the procedure that would be involved if a forensics expert has to perform thinks duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that this would be the order in which a forensics expert would proceed, can you tell us when there is a wound to the body. As a forensics expert, what do you have to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: As a forensics expert that deals with these issues, one has -- one first of all has to establish whether the wound was inflicted by firearms. So you first have to determine the cause of the firearm because you have various kinds of wounds and this is very specific. When you have determined that the wound was caused by a firearm, then it's -- by projectile then you have to describe this with precision. You have to detect the wound with precision, you have to determine where the entry wound is. If there is an exit wound, you have to establish the location of the exit wound, if we're dealing with someone who was killed then all the traces surrounding the wound have to be gathered and analyzed in order to determine what the entry wound is and what the exit wound is and in order to determine the channel of the wound. That is the angle at which the projectile entered the body in relation to the position of the body and this is something that we have to tell the Trial Chambers, Courts. This has to do with the angle of the projectile and the position of the body. I'll illustrate this in the following way because I'll discuss this matter later on. I tried to use the computer to present this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Professor --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'd just like to finish. If we're talking about a fatal wound, it's necessary in such cases to determine the cause of death and to determine whether the cause of death has to do with that wound inflicted from a firearm or whether there were other wounds which caused death and it's necessary to determine everything else relating to the period of death. These are some of the main factors that have to be taken into consideration by a forensic expert all the other kinds of analysis have to be carried out, you have to determine the entry wound, you need to use microscopes, you need to use x-rays of the body or parts of the body and then you compile a report, that's the autopsy report, and this should show whether the procedure was followed and on that basis, you might have relevant evidence. This is why the documents that I had that I have already commented on and this is why I said we only have a report on the diagnosis but it doesn't mention the entry wound and the exit wound and in this case, I wanted to demonstrate this to you. I don't know if we can see it. I can't. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have demonstrated various body positions here and if you are trying to determine the physiological position of the body, the channel would be horizontal but if you are trying to determine the entry wound and the exit wound you can see these two points here, let's say that this is the entry and this is the exit. Now it depends on how the body moves. The channel shall change depending on how the body moves. On this basis it's possible to conclude that we can, if we have determined the position of the body, we can determine from which direction the projectile came and the direction it followed when it passed through the body. This is what has to be performed when carrying out a forensics examination if this examination is to be valid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Your Honours, since we have a few more minutes until the first break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look at the video but first the curtains have to be pulled down. And we return into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session, you may put on the ELMO the sketch you've made, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to make a sketch of the position of the body, bearing in mind the angle, you can see the left side and his back was facing the direction he pointed to with his hand when he was indicating the direction from which the projectile came but according to the medical documentation, the entry was here and it passed through the left part of the body and the channel would then be opposite to the direction of the projectile. The channel would be like this but he indicated that the direction of the projectile was like this. If he was fired at from here, or even if he was fired from this direction, it should have passed through the left hemithorax but the projectile entered at this point as it has been stated in the documents so we have the medical documentation and we have the witness' testimony and it doesn't agree which is why I said that he should be examined in order to define the channel of the wound and in order to ensure that all the elements agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have half an hour, Ms. Pilipovic, to consider the testimony so far. We'll adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could you, while awaiting the expert witness again, could you give us an indication how much time you need because a lot of what the expert witness said, I'm not saying everything, but a lot of what he said is -- comes clearly from his report. I mean that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague also has some questions to ask so we believe he will be for another hour, hour and a half. I don't know how much time my colleague will need. We will try and -- not to repeat what's already been said in the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The insufficiency of, let's say most of the documents in respect of drawing any conclusions by forensic medical expert is not something that should have taken such a long time. There are other very interesting and perhaps new points but I'd rather concentrate on those. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President, I was wondering about the new points. I won't need very much time. I think that if I am very quick it should be about 20 minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time would you need, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I cannot make an assessment. That will depend on the answers of the professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's always true but you could give an assessment on what you expect his average answer to be and you have some influence on the length of the answers, as you are certainly aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that perhaps 40, 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then try to conclude in one hour, all together. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, you told us that you as a medical forensic expert, you have to establish when there is an injury on a body. First of all, considering that you said that it was important to establish the entry and exit wound and how this occurred, could you please tell us, first of all, in your opinion, the entry wound, what does that depend on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The entry wound, a projectile entry wound which is caused by a firearm depends on many factors. One of the factors is the calibre of the projectile. Another factor which is also important is the distance from which the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, my next question would be: What do you get by analysing the distance and how do you conduct analysis of the distance from where the weapon was fired? And if you can be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I'll try. When we are doing a forensic analysis of a distance from where the firearm was fired, first of all, is the entry wound, first what it looks like, whether the projectile arrived, whether it was from a distance or from a nearby location. Another thing which is also to do with the assessment of the distance is also analysing the traces that we can find around the entry wound. Now here, I am showing what a entry wound looks like, a projectile entry wound. As you can see, the entry wound that we have to describe in detail, it's got a tissue injury, it's got a ring around it, it's got traces of gunpowder and this black ring that you can see depends on the angle under which the projectile enters the body. Apart from that, what the entry wound looks like, as I said, also depends on the calibre of the projectile. So what is that projectile the moment as it enters the body. Of course what the entry wound looks like also depends on the velocity of the projectile, the moment of the contact with the body. Slower projectiles make more of a bruising of a tissue and then they injure and then they injure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, what do you get through the analysis of the entry wound, what conclusions can you draw that would be important for your expert report, what do you specifically get by analysing an entry wound?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: By analysing an entry wound, first of all, you get information whether this entry wound happened with a direct hit or whether through an indirect contact. If the projectile changed its direction before hitting the body then you establish a calibre possibly of the projectile itself, after you have to establish the traces, whether this was done from a vicinity or from a distance and what is important which is really to find the exact location of the wound, whether it's on the front of the body, on the side of the body, or the back of the body. In medical documentation that I have so far analysed, I did not have this piece of information in order to answer about an entry wound, where it was, and how it was caused, whether it was projectile or whether this was a fragment of a projectile. When I say a fragment of a projectile which does influence the form of the wound, before it -- before it enters the body, it could be that the jacket falls off and only the jacket of the projectile makes that wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When you gave us your opinion about everything that was needed and why it was needed to have the analysis of -- conducted the analysis of an entry wound, can you tell us, considering that you've told us that when we have bodily injuries, it is also important to establish the direction of the channel of the wound, can you tell us what information is it possible to acquire when you establish the direction of the channel of the wound?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: So apart from the characteristics of the wound, the channel of the wound is one of the pieces of medical information that gives you most -- more other information about the trajectory of the bullet through the body and indirectly we also get the information about how the projectile got to the body, arrived at the body and the channel of the wound is, according to some categories, different. It can be a straight line, if it's only going through soft tissue, it can also be -- it could be cut up, that is when it goes through some organs that change its trajectory through going, then it could be an irregular, for instance if it is deflected by hitting the bone first or it could be in the form of a ring. For instance, when we have injury of a skull, or the issue of the top of the head, what can happen is that when the projectile loses its energy, it goes around, either through the brain or around the brain or around the tissue of the top of the head. Why is that important? It's important because a projectile enters one end and then projectile enters one end and it's found at a different end then it's very important whether this projectile went as a straight line, so that's how the direction would go or this projectile followed a kind of curve. If it went and then it hit a part of a bone, and then it went to the other side of the body, then the channel of the wound is not a straight line. Then we have the entry wound and then into the first obstacle and that then establishes, I'm sorry, but this channel, direction of the channel of the wound not only tells us about the trajectory but also the direction from which the firing came, which is what is vitally important when we are talking about firearm. Can I just give an example, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very brief example. If it's an example, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It's from my personal practical experience. I had an injury and there was a man who was injured and this man was shot in the back by a firearm. It was in the left shoulder-blade. And when he survived, there was a question where the projectile was because there was an x-ray and the projectile couldn't be found and logically it should have either come out or it should have stayed in the thoracic area; however, what happened is that the projectile, while the man was lying down went all the way through the arm and stopped in the hand, the upper part of the hand so the question was: How did it get into the body and how did it come there? So what happened was when there was a shot in the back, the injured was in a -- such a position that the projectile went between the thorax and the shoulder-blade so this is how it went. As I'm showing you now this is what the trajectory of the projectile was so the direction was from that way, not really from the back as would have been logical if he was shot in the back. That's why how important it is to conduct an examination to establish the channel of the injury because that tells you where the direction of the firing came, where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, now you've told us why, in your opinion, it is important to conduct an analysis and to establish the channel of the injury, and why this is important, what we get from it. So what I've understood is the direction from where the bullet came can be established or the projectile, did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, what you're saying, during this testimony, and also in your report, you say that it is necessary to carry out an examination of the person who was allegedly injured by a projectile where there is medical examination in existence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the cases that you've looked at, did you have a situation where there is no medical documentation, have there been such incidents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was medical -- there was such cases, for instance, even when there was cases of death, when we had no medical documentation just the witness testimony, witness statements, where we had no medical documentation we didn't know what kind of injury this was, whether this was a firearm or what kind of weapon this was. I believe that the incident number 5, incident number 6, for instance, where we, for instance, did not know what was the cause of death, what was the location of the injury. We can see that when we go on to speak about these cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are talking about incident number 5 and number 6 when there is no medical documentation, can you tell us in your opinion, what is necessary to have and to do in order to get relevant answers about how the injury occurred?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The doctrine of forensic medicine is that in all death cases, cases of death, it is important, it is necessary to conduct an autopsy. If the autopsy has not been done, then an exhumation has to be carried out and the autopsy done then. But here, when we have most of the medical documentation which is incomplete, and invalid for carrying out such a report, such an analysis, that is absolutely necessary to conduct an examination because it is through the examination that we establish the number of injuries the type of injuries, whether this was firearm, and what type of firearm it was, if possible, and in cause of death, what needs to be done in death cases, you have to carry out an autopsy, all the traces and so on and if you have to do an exhumation then you have to establish what the injuries were on some hard tissue or some soft tissue if there's any left to establish the type and the number of injuries. It is from this data from what is possible to get what can be established that is the distance and the direction of the firing. We establish the channel and the ballistic expert can establish where the fire had come from. So without this relevant medical facts we are not in a position to answer to the simplest questions: The cause of death, how that person died, what injuries he suffered, what was the position of the body when he died, et cetera. So what I'm telling you now, this is our doctrine, all this is reflected also on the people who were not -- who did not die from firearm injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, when you were telling us about the necessity of establishment the -- what the entry and the exit wound looked like, can you tell us is there a difference between the entry and the -- can you, according to what the entry wound looks like, can you establish what type of projectile this was or whether it was a direct hit or whether it was a ricochet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The entry wound gives you most of the information as a rule about the type of the weapon that was used or how the projectile arrived at the body. We know that there are injuries which were -- happen from a distance or from the vicinity and there is a characteristic difference. Whether it's from a close range, from point blank range, we know that the entry wounds are in form star shaped and if it's from a distance we know that these entry wounds are regular but if they are regular if they come under a right angle and then they are -- for instance, if the projectile enters under a right angle, then they are relatively regular, that is the form of a circle but however if it comes under at a different angle then it would be a ellipse. Now if we have a projectile that enters at a right angle, so it's like a circle the projectile has not been damaged when -- before it entered the body in the situation where the projectile doesn't come at a right angle, first it suffered a deformation, perhaps it hit an obstacle or perhaps it's pushing something in front of it then the projectile may suffer a deformation and this deformity will cause the entry wound to be irregular and then it can have different shapes. If the projectile cuts through -- is broken into a jacket and the charge inside the bullet, then these two parts of the projectile can make irregular -- cause irregular wounds or even several wounds apart from this one entry wound so it's very important to establish whether this wound, the entry wound came from a direct contact or not. But if we establish that the entry wounds are of this form then we know that the projectile had hit something in the meantime. If it's a regular form, if it's a circle, then we know it came at a right angle and that it wasn't deformed before it entered the body. So it -- it's on the entry wound we can see what also the type of ammunition that was fired, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, this is important. When you have a pistol bullet which enters a body at the right angle undeformed, undamaged, then the diameter of the entry wound is about 8 millimetre for standard calibre 7.65, however, the rifle 7.62 millimetres, that is, a rifle bullet because of the energy that it carries, will make a much bigger entry wound which the diameter of which is 12 millimetres on average. And what we've done is not -- we haven't done experiments, we -- what we did is that we followed these types of injuries -- depends on the entry wound will type of the entry wound and the velocity of the bullet gets to the body and everything else that I have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. You have told us about the discrepancies between the medical documentation and the testimony or the statement of the witness on the scene of the incident about the direction, according to the victim where the fire came from and also, you've told us that there was a location mentioned in the medical documentation as well. Can you tell us about the cases that you've examined, whether such incidents, other incidents where, according to you, there was medical documentation, but it was contradictory to the statement or the testimony of the witness, that is of the victim?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, if that is the case, we can maybe follow an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about cases number 2, 3?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, for instance, for case number two, I have a -- number 2 I have made some notes. We have the witness statement or testimony, we have some photographs, and that's a film where --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said number 2, in that case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There's no medical documentation. We have a statement which says that the injury was done to the soft tissue of the left thigh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us when you don't have medical documentation, what can you do then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, an examination has to be carried out. Why an examination? Well, first of all to establish whether this was done by a firearm or to locate the entry wound. When you locate the entry wound then we can establish the channel of the wound. And it is from this that we see here where it says in the medical documentation that it was the soft tissue of the right thigh. It doesn't mean anything to me as an expert doesn't mean anything. I cannot answer the question where she has been hit from, whether it's from the vicinity from a distance, where it was entry r exit wound or whether it was just one entry wound I cannot answer any of these questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You've told us now about the incident where there is no medical documentation. Can you tell us your opinion in relation to incidents where you had medical documentation but the victim that was allegedly hurt was not asked for a statement, was not -- did not give a statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to say there was such cases where the witness was not at all hurt.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the leave of the Chamber, I will remind you we had the incidents number 9, number 22, number 25 where the victims were not hurt where there was medical documentation did exist.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to say for instance regarding incident number 9 since I have also made some notes for myself, I have to first point out so far what I have said, I think you can see how relevant it is to hear what the victim and the witness have to say but it's not up to me to say. Up to me, it is to see whether the medical documentation corresponds to the possible statement of the injured party. Now, here we see that there was a injury, exit and entry wound to the left upper leg and we have a police report that says that there was a machine-gun -- there was a burst and that even fragmentation bullets were used and this fire was opened. I don't have a relevant medical documentation to establish fragmentation bullets. What was the entry wound? What was the channel of the wound? And from where this person was fired on in relation to the position that was defined. This person was not -- did not define a position because it wasn't heard about the -- where she was -- where this person was standing. So there is -- so there is nothing that can be said about that. You've also mentioned incident number 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I just ask you what have you now elicited on incident 9 from the expert what is not in his report? It's all what he says in his report. I'm just trying to remind you that let's use the time. The Chamber really reads these reports with great care. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, when you've told us that you have carried out a comparison of medical documentation, and specifically the statement of the victim that was heard or the persons who testified during the trial, your position and you have already stated it in the report, that it is necessary to carry out an examination of the victims. Can you tell us very briefly what would you achieve from an examination and what would you achieve from an exhumation since you said that in cases or in persons in the incidents when there is no medical documentation where death occurred it would be necessary to carry out an exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to somewhat correct you. I cannot say -- you said where there is no medical documentation. There is no medical documentation which is relevant for this kind of report. Even where there is a diagnosis, where there is some medical documentation, I cannot fullfil this report, I cannot answer all the questions, what type of wound that was, whether this was an entry wound or whether it was an entry and exit wound and what was the direction of the channel of the wound and if I don't know that, and if I, for instance, have the testimony of the witness, the statement, I've seen video recording, most of the time, they do not correspond to each other as I have already demonstrated in case number 4 and this is what limits me to give you a full expert report with valid data that you can use. That is why I'm asking, or rather, I'm giving you a suggestion that those who do not have medical documentation, either don't have it at all or it is incomplete, that an examination of living persons should be carried out because -- then the entry wound and the channel that can be established can give us information about what we're talking about. The distance of the firing, the direction of the firing, the number of the injuries and whether these injuries were caused by fragments of projectiles or with complete projectiles, that is what is important. When, in cases of exhumations, where there were no autopsies done, if autopsies were done and we only have an autopsy report which said examination was carried out then I would like to have an autopsy report, a full autopsy report and I would like to comment and perhaps I could then fully comment it, give it -- talk about the trajectory of the direction and the ballistics can confirm. But a person who was not autopsied, a person who was buried from a doctrine point of view from forensics, then all the elements have to be gathered to establish what happened. First of all, whether this person died because of an injury or not. For instance, I think there was a case number 21 that the man died Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. several days later, we don't know why. Was it caused by that injury or because -- or he died because of something else. It could be natural causes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, having mentioned all these observations and your position with regard to providing a complete report, can you tell us how much experience you have with regard to firearms wounds?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I've been involved in forensic medicine for a long time now. Last year, 2002 and 2001, I performed autopsies and made expert reports for over 500 cases in the institute for forensic medicine in Belgrade. This has to do with various kinds of wounds, suicide wounds, firearm wounds, et cetera, and I would like to point out that in the last few years, in the last couple of years I carried out those exhumations in Batajnica and there were over 700 cases of people who had been wounded by firearms and we performed an autopsy for each case. This large number of autopsies, well, I can only compare these orders when I was in Racko, the team leader, the Finnish team leader, Professor Antipentilo [phoen] told me that out of 2.000 autopsies carried out in Helsinki, there were about 40 firearm wounds and if we have 1.500 autopsies at our institute, over 300 cases are cases of people who were wounded by firearms, fatally wounded, not to mention the court cases where people were wounded by firearms but were not killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, we'll -- my colleague will now put a number of questions to you. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Professor. I would like to turn to what you mentioned a minute ago and could you answer to the extent that this is possible by saying yes or no. My first question: Professor, did you make such -- did you compile such reports during the so-called embargo period, the embargo that was imposed on the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, did you write such reports during the so-called bombing period, the so-called bombing period by the NATO forces in the SFRY; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, relevance and leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think it's relevant because if it wasn't I wouldn't ask this question. I'll gladly explain this to you in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The relevance of this issue and something that I mean you ask him whether he did write such reports and the answer will be yes or no, I take it. Is the relevance something -- will he say something in between? You asked him ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer the question that concerns the leading nature of this question, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection was about relevance and not about leading -- or both I have not been -- yes, as far as the leading is concerned, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that objection is denied, the relevance is the issue that -- at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the relevance is quite simple. We know that the former Yugoslavia, that an embargo was imposed on it which was severe and then it was bombed. We know as a result that the circumstances perhaps establish what is sought or perhaps the circumstances on which one wants to determine the position of bodies at possible crime sites it's far more difficult than in normal circumstances and similarly it's possible to establish an analogy with the situation in Sarajevo and I would have liked this witness to tell us whether in spite of the circumstances which are really difficult - being bombed is not very agreeable - I'd like the witness to be able to tell us whether one could establish the position of the bodies and follow a certain procedure and then we could conclude something with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Injuries caused by anything else than what we call sniping incidents? This is a report about shelling or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, no. I expressed myself badly, I apologise. What I meant is that when one is being bombed and when an embargo has been imposed one perhaps doesn't have the necessary means, the technical means, et cetera, the photographic means to carry out one's work and in normal circumstances, it would be easier. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution does not take the position that this expert is not capable of testifying about channel wounds with respect to shooting incidents. The issue is not the quality of his expertise with respect to that field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand, but the question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin was introduced in order to compare the, I would say the possibilities of investigating medical examination of victims under difficult circumstances and to make a comparison. utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So as not to waste time, I'd like to point out to the French booth, page 10, line 12, I don't know if one should say -- Mrs. Pilipovic or something else but it's certainly not Mr. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could not have created any confusion but nevertheless, I appreciate that you made this correction, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.text: Witness, you can you hear me?

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: When the embargo was imposed and when the bombing was carried out, as far as forensic medicine is concerned we adhered to the principles absolutely, we carried out our duties, or the victims, all of those who had been killed or wounded we examined them and compiled valid medical documents from which the relevant conclusions can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you then. My question wasn't whether you managed to carry out your work. My question was whether the conditions were objectively more difficult?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The conditions under which we worked were more difficult absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, I'll stop you there, Professor. Thank you. In spite of these difficulties, am I to take it that you managed to carry out your work and in particular, with regard to the position of the bodies in given incidents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, with regard to this subject, I would like to go back to what you stated and I am referring to page 33 but my computer is blocked. You said that the precise determination of the channel would establish -- would allow one to establish the direction that fire came from; do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, what happens with regard to what you have stated, what you have affirmed if the body is badly positioned, that is to say, to be more precise, if the record does not correctly establish the precise position of the body at the time of the incident? What could the results of this be?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, the results of this, we're talking about an injured party, if we don't have -- if we don't know this position, then we are unable to determine the position from which, let's say the projectile came. We have no basis for determining this because that is only one point in a series from the point -- from the position where the projectile was fired from to the point where the projectile came to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I'll stop you there. utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In these cases?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In these cases, if someone had been wounded, and if the wounded person was taken away from the site immediately because the statements of the witnesses usually say something to this effect, in such cases, it would have been necessary to follow certain procedure later on to determine the location and the position of the person when that person was wounded and one must bear in mind the medical documentation and cooperate with the forensic expert who would determine the nature of the wound and the channel, et cetera. So that would be regardless of the conditions under which this happened. These are things that could be subsequently performed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I'll stop you there, my question is as follows: According to your experience in your field, your professional experience, even in very difficult circumstances, or in difficult circumstances is it possible, by whatever means, to immediately establish, for the sake of the record, what the position of a victim was at a given point in time and if such means do exist, could you tell us what their nature is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question because it's of a local character, of a local nature. What we could do in Belgrade, at home, well, we could establish the traces at the site by photographing the site, by photographing what was there, what was present at the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it possible, was it possible, perhaps, in difficult circumstances, even if this was post mortem, was it possible to establish the trajectory of this channel that you have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this something that requires a kind of infrastructure that would be in relation -- which will have recourse to the means that one could find in cities such as Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is an institute for forensic medicine there and autopsies were performed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a technician here, Mr. President, I appreciate that but this time I didn't request his presence.
